holidays.name: International Chocolate Day
holidays.description: A day for chocolate lovers everywhere to unwrap, melt, nibble and bake. Dark, milk, white, truffles or hot cocoa all count.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial observance. It is often linked to the September 13 birthday of Milton S. Hershey, the American candy maker, who was born in 1857.
holidays.funFact: Cacao beans were once used as currency by the Aztecs, so people were literally spending chocolate.

holidays.name: Roald Dahl Day
holidays.description: A celebration of the master of gloriously twisted children's stories, including Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Matilda and The BFG. Fans mark it by reading, dressing up and inventing their own wacky words.
holidays.origin: The day honors the author's birthday. Roald Dahl was born on September 13, 1916, in Llandaff, Wales, and it has been celebrated by fans and schools since the early 2000s.
holidays.funFact: Dahl invented hundreds of words, such as "scrumdiddlyumptious" and "snozzcumber," and he wrote many of his stories in a garden hut, sitting in a battered armchair.

holidays.name: Uncle Sam Day
holidays.description: A patriotic day honoring the top-hatted, star-spangled symbol of the United States, and the real man believed to have inspired him.
holidays.origin: Samuel Wilson of Troy, New York, was a meat packer who supplied rations to soldiers in the War of 1812. He was born on September 13, 1766, and the soldiers' joke that the "U.S." stamped on his barrels stood for "Uncle Sam" is said to have helped the nickname catch on. Congress recognized him as the namesake of the national symbol in 1961.
holidays.funFact: Uncle Sam's famous "I Want YOU" recruitment poster was painted by James Montgomery Flagg in 1916. Flagg reportedly used his own face as the model, with some added age and a white beard.
